utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Our start was delayed due to some logistical problems. And we are sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis probably for the first session with Judge Morrison being away who is now flying from London this morning. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Colonel, I want to start today by talking about the 10th Sabotage Detachment to go over a couple of things you've said in your statement and previously. Just, first of all, you were the superior officer in charge of this detachment in the professional chain; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, professional control and command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as I understand your statement in paragraph 18, you -- what that means is that you propose their use somewhere, and then it's up to General Mladic to say yes or no; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then if General Mladic orders the unit can take action, it's your job as their professional superior to make sure his orders are carried out; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that they're implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the unit's operations are monitored, not necessarily by you directly but by intelligence officers in the subordinate units and they would be providing you with reports on the operation; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could see that here also, I would issue directives and also a briefing so that I could assure myself of the level of competence and to make sure that the assignment could be carried out without losses or with minimal casualties and so on and so forth. Then I would issue the permission to start with the implementation of the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And after an operation, it would be normal for the detachment to brief you; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the detachment commander would submit a report and the intelligence officer from the corps, for example, who was there directly with him would monitor the organisation of that assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that report isn't necessarily a written report. You could have a conversation, an oral briefing; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Just to go on to another topic. And it's from the evidence you gave in the Mladic case last week. Can you confirm last week you said your service was aware of the situation in Srebrenica up to 90 per cent, and that was at transcript page 13089. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it was aware of the situation in Srebrenica, that it was aware of the situation, this is a term that I did not use. That is not my term. This is a term used by the interpreter. Therefore, my service was aware of the situation in Srebrenica almost to the degree of 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We continuously monitored the situation in Srebrenica throughout the whole war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you did that in a number of ways. You did that through electronic reconnaissance, you had direct information, you told the Mladic Judges that you actually had a man inside, and you would receive information from subordinate units; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I want to talk about directives now for a minute, and you talked about them when you testified here before, in the Tolimir case. And you told my colleague Mr. McCloskey that you might have participated in the planning of two or three of those directives, and that was in the Tolimir case at transcript page 13494. So I'd like to know which ones?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean throughout the war, throughout the whole period of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you told Mr. McCloskey you might have participated in the planning of two or three directives. So which ones were those? Did you -- I don't want to interrupt your train of thought.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, now -- yes, there was one directive for activities in the Sarajevo sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, every directive carried instructions for activities in the Sarajevo area, so maybe what I could do is show you a couple of them to see if that jogs your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at P976.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's a directive for further operations number 4 dated 19 November 1992. Now, this first paragraph of this document, General, looks very much like it has a large intelligence component to it. Did you participate in the drafting of this directive, do you remember? And I can tell you that --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually I would do the first item, but it wasn't a rule in each directive. Some directives were drafted at the level of the corps, and then the corps intelligence organ would participate in the drafting, not me. For example, directly it could refer to Sarajevo. For example, the directive for Srebrenica is one I never did participate in. It was drafted at the level of the corps, therefore -- well, specifically I would now need to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is this one of the directives you participated in the drafting of, from 11 November -- pardon me, from 18 November 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been -- I'm not ruling it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about we go and look at another one quickly, P977. Let's just jump over a year to 25 June 1993. And this is directive for further operations number 5, and we can stay on the first page but I'll tell you, Colonel, that paragraph 5(A) of this document, and it's in English page 3 and B/C/S page 5, tasks the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, among other things, to take control of Trnovo and the Sarajevo-Trnovo road and the wider area between Treskavica and Jahorina and Igman and Bjelasnica, and to take the dominant feature on Igman and Bjelasnica to create conditions for the take-over of Sarajevo and the linking of Herzegovina with RS territory. So this has a pretty significant component related to Sarajevo. Did you participate in the drafting of this directive?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, I did. The first item, the one that contains information about the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to another one and we're going to jump over to the end of 1993. It's P4925. And that's an amendment to directive number 6 dated -- I think we'll probably have to make it a little bit bigger if we can on the B/C/S side for the Colonel. Dated December 1993, and it's issued as a result of or immediately following and as a result of the meeting you attended on 12 December with Dr. Karadzic that I showed you on Friday of last week in General Mladic's diary. And this first paragraph that says basic characteristics of the international political and military situation, that comes from the intelligence administration; right? That reflects your input --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to go on to directive number 7. You alluded to that a couple of minutes ago in your testimony, and that's P838. Now, you've seen this directive before during your different testimonies here and you were shown it in the Tolimir case. Now, in your statement, Colonel, at paragraph 19 you said you only heard about this directive much later than March 1995 when Colonel Lazic, a Drina Corps operative, told you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But in the Tolimir case you were actually more expansive in your answer, and what you said was you learned of this directive in 1997, when Lazic told you. He was one of the ones who participated in its drafting, and I'm going to quote your answer to you so please listen carefully. You said: "I suppose" --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "I suppose that it was done by the commanders in a circle of his assistants. I believe that a lot of intel information went into this directive and that it could have been obtained from the Drina Corps, and in the ops room there was a detailed intelligence map which was updated every day by intel officers. And if you consulted the computer, you could have the updated information on Srebrenica and Zepa in five minutes, and that could have been provided to either Tolimir or Miletic. That was our obligation. We as intelligence officers were obliged to do that without even knowing what the purpose of the exercise was." And that was at the Tolimir transcript, page 13497. So my question, Colonel, is: From that answer it sounds like the document, this directive, reflects input from both the Main Staff intelligence administration and the Drina Corps level; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you testified about this document in the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Kos case, on 13 May 2011, you were even more detailed. And just one question about the -- your testimony in the Kos case. You swore an oath there to tell the truth, right, just like you did here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Maybe we could have a look at a page of the transcript of your testimony from that trial. It's 65 ter number 25267, pages 21 and 22. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your indulgence for a moment. Mr. Registrar, could you go down to the bottom of the page. I might have written the actual page number -- right down to the bottom so I can see the page number. Thank you. And if we can stay there at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is in English, Colonel, so I'm going to read to you the question you were asked and the answer you gave, and it was about Directive 7 and the operation of the Bosnian Serb army being prepared to be launched against Srebrenica. You said -- or the question was: "Were you aware of the operation of the Vojska Republika Srpska to be launched ... being prepared to be launched against Srebrenica?" And you said: "No. I was informed of it in the ICTY when I was there in 2004. They told me about the alleged plan and the directive of the Supreme Command, I didn't know about it back then. I didn't know of it and I didn't participate," if we could go over to the next page, please, "I didn't participate in its devising or planning or anything else in this regard. And when I returned from the ICTY, I asked Lazic, the Operations Officer in the Corps, and he said that there was such a thing, that the President had visited them and that they were preparing this directive of some sort, that it was prepared at the level of the Main Staff and being distributed further to the level of the Corps." So that's what you said. Can you confirm that's true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it was prepared, no, no, no, no. Something is not quite right here. It was prepared at the corps command. It's correct that the president also came and it was prepared there, the assignments were given. As for the Main Staff, the duty operations officer from the Main Staff can always get information from my administration. He doesn't have to say what it's about. All needs to do is to say that he's interested in the disposition of forces and the intention of the enemy in the sector of Srebrenica and that's it. So he could always have that or in any other part of Republika Srpska. So something is not quite ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What's not right about this answer? Is it true what I just read back to you you said, or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that directive being planned at the Main Staff at all, so I don't know how I could have said that it was planned at the Main Staff and passed to the Drina Corps command. This is why I asked Lazic: "Is it true that there was a directive?" He said that it was and that they drafted it, that the president of republika came to them and that it was drafted there at the corps command. As for how others understood that and wrote it down, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're leaving Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Salapura, I'm going to read out what you just said. It's at transcript page 8 and from lines 9: "It was prepared at the corps command. It's correct that the president also came and it was prepared there. The assignments were given." What did you mean by "it"? What was prepared at the corps command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean by "directive"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A directive is a directive. A directive is issued from the level of the Supreme Command or from the level of the Main Staff. And then beyond that, there would be an order for combat. That's the name of the document, that's what the document is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when you said it was prepared at the corps command, did you mean that directive of the Supreme Command or the order -- [overlapping speakers] -- just order for combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "directive." It clearly states "directive," or rather, it is a directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard of Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you said the president came to the Drina Corps and prepared something, did you mean Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Krivaja 95 is the coded name of that. I'm not saying it was just the president who was there. Probably somebody was there from the Main Staff, the duty operations officer, the Chief of Staff, the commander. I don't know who took part in the preparation of that directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. You -- just to be clear, Mr. Salapura, you said: "Krivaja 95 is the coded name of that." What is "that" again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is -- that is the name of that operation, the coded name, the encrypted name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let me be clear. So "Krivaja 95" is the name of the directive or the order for combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the directive. A directive is written for the execution of those actions, and the operation would be called by the coded name of Krivaja 95. Operations are executed and a directive is a directive. An operation would be carried out and it would be bearing that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it at that. Back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, in your statement you talked about this preventive or pre-emptive action by the 10th Sabotage Detachment in Srebrenica in 1995, but you didn't give us any details about it. So I want to get you to confirm your evidence about that action that you gave in the Tolimir case. What you said there was that General Krstic had requested approval for the operation from General Mladic and General Mladic personally asked you to review the operation or the situation and see whether it was feasible; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so you went to the Drina Corps command, and there you met Milorad Pelemis, the detachment commander, and the Drina Corps security chief --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- and the Drina Corps security chief Vujadin Popovic --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's the same Vujadin Popovic who was also convicted of genocide, extermination, murder, and persecutions for his role in the Srebrenica killings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Pavle Golic was also at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you heard their plan and you gave your recommendations to Mladic, and the operation was approved by General Krstic and General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at 65 ter number 25096.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, you've seen this document before dated 21 June 1995 when you've testified here previously. That's your order for this operation; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 1 of this document says that the command of the 10th Sabotage Unit Detachment and the chief of the Drina Corps intelligence department, that's Kosuric; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but at that time he wasn't there so his assistant Golic attended instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It says -- this document says that Pelemis and Kosuric are going to be responsible for collecting information, planning, and carrying out the task, but you said Golic replaced Kosuric in that regard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Golic was present at that particular meeting that I held, but at this meeting Golic was not present. I'm referring to this conversation and deliberation and the drafting of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 3. It says: "Co-ordination between the units in contact will be done by the Chief of the Drina Corps Intelligence Department and he will take charge of the whole action." Paragraph 4 says: "Inform the Drina Corps Chief of Staff..." And that was General Krstic at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Inform General Krstic about the task, and General Krstic is serving 35 years in prison for aiding and abetting genocide; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in your statement you didn't give the date of this operation, but it happened overnight on 23 to 24 June 1995, about two weeks before the attack on the enclave of Srebrenica began; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment plus a unit of the Bratunac Brigade passed through an old mining tunnel into the town centre in the dead of night between 2.00 and 4.00 in the morning in what you described in your Tolimir evidence as low visibility because of fog and armed with infantry weapons fired into the town?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I go further, could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25096 receives number P6408, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So after firing into the town, the units pulled back into VRS territory through the tunnel. Now, what you called a restrictive action in your statement you described as muscle flexing during your testimony in the Tolimir case. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't speaking about any muscles. I said that that was a diversionary action and the assignment of very precise tasks in order to determine and identify the targets. There was the brigade and the police station and at 4.00 in the morning we identified the targets and the timing and we took care that there was only a person on duty there without any other personnel present in order to avoid casualties. And we knew that at that particular time of day there was fog often present that would decrease visibility and that we would opt for diversionary actions only that would last for a few minutes. And it was emphasised that we should try to avoid any casualties among UNPROFOR or civilian population, i.e., women, children, and the others. This action was to be understood as a warning so that the opposing side in Srebrenica be made to stop their continuous sabotage and ambush actions and attacks coming from that area against the positions of the VRS territory because we were constantly incurring casualties as a result. That was a warning for them to give up on that; however, two days after this operation they carried out a counter-action against the territory of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's stay on this operation. I'm going to take you back to exactly what you said in the Tolimir case. You said, after giving the explanation you've just given, you said --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- "we wanted to flex muscle and show them that we were capable of launching similar operations." So, Colonel, in circumstances -- let me just finish, Colonel, I'll give you every opportunity to answer. In circumstances which were such that you shouldn't have carried out an attack, in a town crowded with civilians, in a UN protected area, in darkness, fog, with no visibility, your only objective was to scare the people inside the area, like you said, to flex muscle?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, please. The phrase "flexing a muscle" is something that I never used. It may have been just an arbitrary interpretation by the interpreters, and that was not the meaning of this operation. The meaning of this operation was to warn the opposing side to stop their operations and to make it known to them that we are also capable of carrying out similar operations, and for that reason you can see that it's written there that all measures ought to be taken in order to avoid civilian casualties among women and children, UNPROFOR members, and so on and so forth. So the purpose of that action was not the one as you are representing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if we accept your version of the -- or your explanation of the objective behind the operation, it didn't even matter whether or not there were civilian casualties, Colonel. Your objective was to scare the people in Srebrenica, to intimidate them, and make sure they understood they weren't even safe inside their homes because they never knew when you were going to come out and shoot at them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, the action was not aimed at the civilian population and intimidating them. You know that the command of the 28th Division was in Srebrenica and that there were about 8.000 members in Srebrenica, and you also know that this zone had never been demilitarised. You know that our population and our troops were constantly being killed and they were seeking shelter from UNPROFOR; however, this position was abused. Nobody would ever have had attacked Srebrenica had it been demilitarised and had the agreement been observed, and I particularly refer to this operation which was strictly restricted in its purpose and we had a very specific aim that we set and that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 15, from line 22 through 24, it is not clear who sought protection from UNPROFOR. The witness said that our people were killed and that the Muslims, after these killings, sought protection from UNPROFOR, that they returned to the enclave seeking protection from UNPROFOR. And as the transcript indicates, it seems that it was the Serbs who were asking UNPROFOR to provide protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can understand correctly. Let's continue -- but, Ms. Edgerton, when was this attack?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have the line reference for you, but 23/24 June, overnight between -- from 23 to 24 June 1995, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this action or an attack part of the criminal activities in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And talking about the objectives where you just responded to my question, Colonel, I'd like us to go back to Directive 7 for a second, that's P838 again. And once we see it, to go over to English transcript page -- English page 8 and B/C/S page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. Your indulgence, I just need to check the page reference because I don't see the right page reference here and that's my mistake. But I can go without referring to the document because I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 10 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And it would be under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Drina Corps you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Colonel, just out of courtesy I want to find you the corresponding page in B/C/S, and it's completely my fault that we can't find it right now. Paragraph 6. It might be page 15 in B/C/S. E-court page 15. So my apologies, Colonel. Under the tasks for the Drina Corps that we see in this document, and you're familiar with this because you've studied this document before, you see that the specific tasks for the Drina Corps include "by planned and well-thought-out combat actions to create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." So, Colonel, if we were to accept your explanation of the objectives of this tunnel operation, that operation is completely consistent with the language of this directive, isn't it? It was one more step for making life for civilians in the pocket unbearable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check whether we are on the correct page in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask my colleague behind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My colleague behind me advises we're on the correct B/C/S page but we don't -- and he says it's in the middle of the page, that's the heading that we see halfway through the B/C/S, Drinski Korpusa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's -- the box I just read out, Your Honour, is the first whole paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- by the heading "Drinski Korpusa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat my question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we were to accept your explanation of the objectives of this tunnel operation, that would make it completely consistent with the language of this directive. It was one more step, that operation, in making life for civilians in the pocket unbearable?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, earlier we spoke about this sabotage action and it has nothing to do with this directive. I was not either the creator or the author of this directive. Let us be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question is: Isn't the objective of this operation consistent with the language of this directive. This directive commands that Drina Corps forces make life -- create an unbearable situation of total insecurity for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa, and that's exactly what the tunnel operation was aimed at; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot establish a connection with -- between the tunnel operation and this operation. There is no connection whatsoever between the two no matter how hard you try to do that. I never wrote this directive. I may have received some information about the enemy from my operatives. I was not a commander and I didn't make any such -- after all, this operation, you have my testimony in the Tolimir case, when I said, if you remember, that when I set off on 25th to undergo medical treatment, and he asked me on that occasion what I thought about the enclaves of Zepa, Srebrenica, Gorazde, and so on and so forth. I responded by saying - and you can find this - that I did not think that we should touch any of the enclaves at all. And he agreed that the enclaves were like ripe pears and that he shared my opinion, and later on a decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 11, Colonel said 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So General Tolimir agreed that the enclaves were like ripe pears and that he shared your opinion, and later on a decision was taken. A decision was taken to do what? What did you mean, Colonel, when you said a decision was taken? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decision to attack. I'm talking about a decision to attack Srebrenica which was taken later, but it has nothing to do with this diversionary activity that was aimed at Srebrenica. I'm not a commander. I'm not a decision-maker or someone who issues orders. I did not propose the engagement of our own forces nor did I propose any engagement and tasks. You see what's written here, so please do not add anything to it and do not make any presumptions. It is very accurately written as to what the 10th Sabotage Detachment was supposed to do in terms of its tasks by going through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, where did you -- where exactly did you monitor this operation from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this one? I never followed this operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, Colonel, you saw Pelemis the very morning after the operation was carried out, and he briefed you about the operation. Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you mean the operation when the detachment entered the tunnel? I think I was in Vlasenica, but I cannot say that I'm 100 per cent sure. I was at the command post in Crna Rijeka, but I think I was in Vlasenica at the time when Pelemis came and submitted a report. So I make a reservation that a mistake is possible as far as this information is concerned after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just -- wonder if I could have some guidance about when we might have our breaks today given our delayed start for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is okay with the parties, the Chamber is minded to adjourn at 3.00 for today. So if it's possible, can we go for a further 15 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the first break at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit now about your trip to Belgrade, Colonel, because you only told us about the way back in your statement and not about how the trip came about and the way there. So, first of all, maybe you can confirm, you were in Banja Luka when Srebrenica fell; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Banja Luka. Let me just think a bit because you are switching to something else, but okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you travelled to Belgrade on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Excuse me, I have to tell you right now that I'm not sure whether I went on the 11th or the 12th. After all this time, I do still think that we set off early on the morning of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you went there -- you travelled there with two IT specialists from your intelligence centre in Banja Luka and a driver, right, your driver?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were IT people, engineers versed in electronics and information technologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What were the names of the two IT specialists and your driver?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One IT engineer was Mirko Obradovic, the other IT engineer was called Braco. Give me some time to remember. And the name of the driver was Radan Djukic. Braco Erceg. Braco Erceg.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you talk about the intelligence centre in Banja Luka, you're talking about the 410th Intelligence Centre; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only one that existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And coming from the 410th Intelligence Centre, the people you travelled with would have had information about the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people? These people have nothing to do with that. They deal with completely different things, electronics, the installation of programme, and so on, technical equipment, computers. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So why were they travelling with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they become involved in analysis a bit. Well, they went to install these programmes, and I was supposed to give them a ride to Bijeljina. And then from Bijeljina, from the centre, they were supposed to be taken to Han Pijesak, and then that is where they were supposed to install a new programme at the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you set off on the morning of the 12th and you travelled to Belgrade first via Modrica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then you stopped in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, first in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then you stopped -- so you stopped in Modrica and then you stopped in Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're interested in why I stopped in Modrica, I can tell you. There was a group from the detachment that was there too, the 10th, that was supposed to carry out an assignment there. The officer who was in charge of that asked that someone come. When he viewed the situation, he thought that there might be civilian casualties and he asked for permission to stop with the implementation of that task. He presented that to me and I accepted his explanation. That task was given up on and the unit continued reconnaissance for our unit that was operating in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually, Colonel, you've already given evidence in the state court -- pardon me. You've already given evidence, both in the Tolimir case and in the state court, to the effect that the unit in Modrica called you on the 11th because they weren't able to contact Pelemis and called you through the 410th Intelligence Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then Kremenovic - and this is in your statement before the state court - Kremenovic, the officer you've just --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- just referred to --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- told you that Srebrenica had fallen and that the other part of the 10th Sabotage Detachment had been engaged in the operation; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you in your statement said that in August 1995 you spoke with Pelemis about the participation of the 10th Sabotage Unit in Srebrenica and he confirmed the unit was engaged in combat at the beginning of the operation, that wasn't the first time you knew about it by any stretch?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that I found out immediately in Modrica, but I hadn't seen Pelemis personally until the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us the para number or page where he talked about hearing from Pelemis for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page -- it should be paragraph 8, Your Honour, page 22 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here he said: "I spoke with detachment commander Pelemis about the participation in the Srebrenica events." And he confirmed the engagement in combat action at the beginning of the operation. So here he talked about Srebrenica events, not necessarily limiting to the first part of the operation. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And maybe we should just stay with this area for a little while, actually, and come back to the travel to Belgrade later just so we can flesh this out. Because these, Colonel, are some of the changes you made to your final statement, and you did that by way of a clarification to your evidence in the Tolimir case. So in the Tolimir case at transcript pages 13593 to 13594, you were asked: "So are you saying that it wasn't until sometime after his arrest," referring to Drazen Erdemovic, "on 2 March 1996 that you learned that people were murdered by the VRS?" And your answer was: "Yes, when it was published in the press then the stories began." And in your Tolimir testimony you then said you called Pelemis and had the conversation you describe at paragraph 8 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then in your statement you say, as His Honour Judge Kwon just indicated, in August 1995 you spoke with Pelemis about the participation of the 10th Sabotage Unit in the Srebrenica events and he confirmed the engagement in combat actions at the beginning of the operation. And then you say in your statement that following your testimony in the Tolimir case you established more precisely that it was in late December 1995 when you knew that the 10th Sabotage Detachment had been involved in executions. And that's when you had the conversation with Pelemis that you elaborate on. So let's go back to your conversation with Pelemis in August 1995 first. That's when he was in the Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: August 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- oh, August, yes. In August he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He was in the Krajina because you had detached the unit there; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I. He went to the Krajina in accordance with the decision of the commander. I suggested to the commander that the detachment be transferred to that zone. The commander issued an order and I just conveyed that order, but please just one correction. I would kindly ask -- actually, this group of soldiers who were on leave, however, the detachment did not take part in the execution and the top people, the leaders of the detachment did not, so I would kindly ask that you speak about a group of people not the detachment because it wasn't the entire detachment. This was a small group of people who at the time were on leave and who had nowhere to go, home or wherever. They stayed there and that's how ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, when you refer to the commander, do you mean to refer to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talked to Pelemis in the Krajina in August 1995, what did he tell you had gone on in Srebrenica? How members of the 10th Sabotage Unit were involved? And, General --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not talk about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, Colonel. Understanding that by this time there was widespread public outcry about the missing men and boys from Srebrenica, and you would have known that because part of your job was to monitor the media. So setting that in place, what did -- let's change the question around. What did you ask Pelemis? Let's hear it, General -- Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not talk about that at all. I was in the Krajina. We were at Ostrelj between Bosanski Petrovac and Drvar. I just asked him, "Why were you involved in Srebrenica when the detachment was supposed to go to Herzegovina?" - this other group that was there was supposed to go and reconnoitre in Herzegovina. His answer was, "On orders from the commander," that is to say -- well, Zivanovic -- no, Krstic. Krstic I think asked that that part of the detachment that had stayed on be involved for entering into town and the commander approved that. Go back to Ostrelj. Our conversation at Ostrelj lasted five minutes. We were in a very difficult situation there. Krajina, the Republic of the Serb Krajina, part of it in Croatia, had already fallen and then there were further operations, an attack against Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and no one --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm not asking you about the context. You can tell Dr. Karadzic about that all you like. I'm asking you about the conversation. You knew, Colonel, at the least, by the 12th of July, that members of the 10th Sabotage Unit had been involved in the fall of Srebrenica. The night of the 13th of July you were in contact with unit headquarters in Vlasenica to find out what was going on. By the -- by the 18th of July, you knew from the media that there was widespread international outcry about the loss of the men and boys in Srebrenica, and your evidence is you didn't ask Pelemis what happened when you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, certainly not then, not from the media or anything. We did not have any media then except newspapers of Republika Srpska. In the eastern part of Republika Srpska, there was no electricity. We didn't know anything, and I did not know truly. And then, that is to say up until the end of July, I was still undergoing medical treatment and then General Mladic called me to come to Ostrelj and that's what I did then if that matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume at 17 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I believe Judge Morrison will join us in the next session. Yes, please carry on, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, just to go back to what you said before we broke, you said that: "We didn't have any media then except newspapers of Republika Srpska," and "In the eastern part of Republika Srpska, there was no electricity." And that's one of the reasons why you didn't know about the killings of men and boys in Srebrenica; is that right? You didn't know because there was no electricity in the eastern part of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even in the western part, even more than in the eastern one. I don't know where you got that from. That's not the only reason. I said that we were absolutely oriented towards the situation in the western part and that was the final operation, and after that there was no talk about that. I don't know of any intensive -- well, probably it started later in the Muslim media. I don't know exactly when, I cannot say, but we considered this to be propaganda. I -- I considered it. I'm speaking about myself. No one talked about that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was only --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- General -- Colonel, pardon me, not only was there no electricity in the eastern part of Republika Srpska in July and August 1995, you just said there's no electricity in the western part as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go to a document and it wasn't on my initial notification to the parties. It's just arisen as a result of the Colonel's answers immediately before the break and we've sent out a notification as soon as I was able to locate the document. It's 65 ter number 06664.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's available in your language as well, Colonel. Colonel, this is -- I'll just wait until it's enlarged in English. This is a copy of a statement that was issued on the 17th of July, 1995, by Jovan Zametica, and you know who he is, don't you, he was President Karadzic's -- one of President Karadzic's advisors.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's a statement that was issued on SRNA and it was picked up by Belgrade SRNA and it says -- it's his denial of Muslim media and world reports on events in Srebrenica. And it says: "Over the past few days, the world media assisted and prompted by Muslim authorities have indulged in an orgy on the uncritical events in Srebrenica and lists some of the allegations." And then says: "The truth is that nothing like that happened." And if we could go over to the next page in this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure it has second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not even in English, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mistake in my upload, but I can still continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, this statement was issued over Banja Luka Srpska Televizija on the 17th of July, 1995. It was picked up by SRNA in Belgrade, it was later picked up by the CNN. So, Colonel, in Pale, not only did they have electricity there receiving media reports of what happened in Srebrenica. They're denying media reports of what happened in Srebrenica. France, England, and America knew what was going on in Srebrenica, and you're saying you don't because Banja Luka had no electricity?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was not in Banja Luka on the 17th of July. I came to Banja Luka on the 18th. On the 13th I was in Han Pijesak, or rather, on the 17th I was in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Where do you have the Banja Luka television here?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In this document it's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The last paragraph says -- it says Zametica's statement forwarded to SRNA, not mentioning the television.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, if I -- that's correct, but I can, in the interests of time I proceeded that way. I can provide a 65 ter number for the document referring to Banja Luka in a couple of moments as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, are you saying that there was no electricity in Han Pijesak now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Han Pijesak there was electricity coming from generators, the generators operated so the radio communications -- our communications equipment was working because we had the oil-fuelled generator that was operating.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, on what basis are you saying that there was no electricity in eastern and western Republika Srpska in July and August?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the entire area. I cannot say. I mean, after all these years, sometimes it does, sometimes it doesn't. Now you're asking me to guess about every day and minute, but generally there was this problem. It was Banja Luka that mostly remained without electricity, but the army had generators. And I, from the 18th of July, was on sick leave and I was being treated at home again. I interrupted that sick leave. I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, you've just said now again that Banja Luka mostly remained without electricity, and maybe we could go to the news report for Banja Luka that I've since found. 65 ter number 00689. Here you see, Colonel, the initial statement by Jovan Zametica carried on Banja Luka Srpska Televizija on 17 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Zametica is making a statement on TV which isn't going to work if they don't have any electricity, Colonel. So with respect, Colonel, what are you talking about? Banja Luka knew because Zametica, Dr. Karadzic's advisor, is here denying the killings at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Pale and the authorities there seem to be better informed than you were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The press media --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Most of the witness's answer was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, could you repeat your question. Interpreters were not able to hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that that is possible too. It is possible. I cannot remember now these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Without interrupting the Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I do not rule out that possibility because I know that most people, also from the Main Staff, consider that to be almost impossible even when they did hear about it. I used to think that that was impossible too, but you see it was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 06664 will be Exhibit P6409 and 00689 will be Exhibit P6410.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before we go back to your travels to the enclave, I still want to stay on the subject of your conversations with Pelemis whenever you might have had them.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, when you heard the answer from Pelemis that you've discussed in your statement, that whoever might have been involved in the executions had volunteered, you were basically satisfied with that answer; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not satisfied. I was not satisfied. I just said to him whoever had not only participated but whoever had engaged these people, involved them, should be held responsible. I used one of our words, jargon: Who feels an itch should scratch himself. I don't know if this can be interpreted literally. I don't know if the interpreters can do a literal interpretation or translation of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You told him to get the people who were involved to write statements, and your evidence is you don't know what happened after that or whether the statements were ever written; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after that I said that I did not know whether they wrote it or whether they gave him statements about that because I think he was on annual leave then and then he handed over his duty. And then I also went on annual leave after that and then we did not have any contact about that. At the end of his annual leave he left, he handed over his duty and left, and yes, 1996, yes. 1996, beginning of 1996. I used my annual leave and then I had some time when I was entitled not to be assigned to a particular post, and then I submitted my request for retirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, you know, Dr. Karadzic is calling a witness, Franc Kos who was -- you would know, he was -- that's the trial that you went to testify on in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was a commander in one of the 10th Sabotage Unit's platoons, and he's coming to talk about the executions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I want to show you an interview he had with Dr. Karadzic's Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- on 6 March 2013, and it's 65 ter number 1D07999.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your indulgence for a moment again. I didn't realise there was an uploaded translation, so what I'm going to have to do is find the B/C/S page reference to what I want to direct us to out of courtesy to the Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go, though, to pages -- starting at page 21 in English. Actually, in English we could go over to page 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll tell you this in --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll tell you this in summary, Colonel, and as soon as I have the page reference in your language I'll give it to you so you can follow along. But Mr. Kos was at the base of the 10th Sabotage Detachment when he received two calls from Colonel Beara on the morning of the 16th of July, 1995, telling him to take seven soldiers and to come to the corps command in Vlasenica. And there was no one at the base at that moment. But about an hour later, Pelemis, Dragomir Pecanac, and the full complement of the 2nd Platoon arrived as well as some soldiers of the 1st Platoon who had been on leave. Mr. Kos was eventually called to Pelemis's office, and there he found Pelemis, Pecanac, and Zoran Obrenovic, and Pecanac then said to him, "You and seven soldiers are going today to guard the prisoners." And they went from there to Branjevo, where they then executed the prisoners? So, Colonel, that doesn't sound like anyone volunteered for the task; they received an order from Pelemis. So, Colonel, either Pelemis wasn't telling you the truth or what you're telling us today isn't accurate. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before you answer further --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, out of courtesy, page 17 in B/C/S for the Colonel. And I think you found it for us already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think previous page seems to be the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The previous page was the correct one. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, let him read it. Shall we collapse the English first for some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let Mr. Salapura read it in full. Tell us when you are done and we'll show you the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't say this to me. I am seeing these details for the very first time. I didn't know the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to read further? I think it continues on the next page. Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that on the 15th of -- and 16th of July you didn't know really what any part of the 10th Sabotage Unit was doing; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All I know is that I knew when I came on the 13th I was told that the duty operations officer had called, that that group that stayed in the base, that that group participated in the combat in Srebrenica, that they were given rest, that the soldiers went home, the security remained there, and a group of soldiers who had nowhere to go. Later when I spoke with Miso in December, he told me what I said in my statement and I stand by that. I didn't call them anymore after the 13th, I didn't call them anymore. Pelemis went with an APC. He told me that on the 13th they had an accident. The car crashed, and he was hurt. He went for treatment and then he got some sort of sick leave or something and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence then is that you had no contact with the unit or any members of the unit after they participated in the killings at Bisina under the command of Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until Ostrelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You had no contact with them after their duty in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until Ostrelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Even though it's procedure - and you said it was - for the commander to brief you after the conclusion of an operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is a part of the operation in which I had no part. This is not part of the tasks of the unit. This is part of indirect duties. This is something that probably was a result of direct engagement by the commander of the Main Staff. I said that I came on the 13th to that area, that I found General Mladic in Srebrenica, and I had come to inform him about what was ahead of us and I wanted to come back the next day, and I wasn't able to for health reasons. And then the next day the road was already closed, so I was unable to return until the 18th. The road was closed from Han Pijesak towards Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's have a look, Colonel, at 65 ter number 25271, please. Colonel, this is a document from you dated 15 July 1995, ordering the rear command post of the VRS Main Staff to approve paint for two terrain vehicles for the 10th Sabotage Detachment. So the day before they go on operations at Branjevo you're actually --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You issued this. So, Colonel, you had to have been in contact to issue this order, otherwise you wouldn't have been aware of any need. You wouldn't have been aware that they needed paint?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- yes, I was at the command post at the time. This is their logistics guy, most probably, who sent a request to us for intervention --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please, Colonel, your last sentence. The interpreters weren't able to understand.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This request was most probably sent to us by the detachment logistics person. He sent it to the administration. On the 15th, since I was at the command post, I signed it and I forwarded it to the logistics organ or the technical sector of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6411, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we go any further. Ms. Edgerton, in -- at page 37, line 21, you said even though it's procedure and you said it was for the commander to brief you after the conclusion of an operation. What operation did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was referring to the witness's evidence at the beginning of his testimony, where I asked him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's operation on the 22nd or the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But he spoke generally at the outset of his testimony in that regard, Your Honours, and said that after an operation it would be normal for the detachment to brief him. So I was referring back to the testimony he gave at the -- the testimony he gave at the outset of the proceedings today. And he did subsequently confirm that he received a briefing from Pelemis after the operation on the 23rd and 24th of June as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did he confirm that he had received briefing either Pelemis or anybody above Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not so far, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to go to the testimony of someone else in the Kos case, the case that you testified in, 65 ter number 25280 is the transcript or is the transcript of the evidence of Petar Cvjetinovic. And if we could go, please, over to page 27 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could scroll down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll read this slowly for you, Colonel. And Petar Cvjetinovic was a member of the Panteri. He was asked by Dusko Tomic: "When did you learn about the events in Srebrenica and if you could briefly to the Court what was the nature of your participation in Srebrenica?" And he answered: "I'm not sure if it was the 15th or 16th July, I think it happened on the 15th and attorney Tomic told me that this was on 16th ... a driver of Petar Salapura found me in Bijeljina." And if we could go over to the next page, please. He's asked: "Who was the driver?" Response: "Zoran Bogdanovic." And Mr. Tomic says: "All right, and what happened next?" And then the witness says: "He asked that I should come to the private house, a private house of Bijeljina businessman Savo Jovanovic, and there was a basement in this house and the military security service had tapping service in the basement, and Panteri unit was also using the personnel there. I found a Colonel Petar, Petar Salapura there. I think he was a colonel at that time, and he talked to me, and Milorad Pelemis was also there. He was also present, and Zoran Manojlovic was another person who was present there." Mr. Tomic asks who these individuals were. And the witness said: "Petar Salapura, I don't know exactly his position, but I know that he was a member of the military security service of the Vojska Republika Srpska. Zoran Manojlovic was a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment and responsible for the security as far as I know, and Miso Pelemis, he was the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment." And he's asked: "What happened next when you came there? "Salapura talked to me," he responded, "he told me that I was the ideal person to do a service to Republika Srpska. He explained to me that during the attack on Srebrenica there was murder, there was killing of several thousand Muslim civilians, soldiers, and there were already images circulating in the world that this had happened. And he said that I could be of help." And then the witness continues and says: "Petar Salapura told me that I was the ideal person to go to the military farm in Branjevo, and members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment were to arrive there. I don't know from where, but later on I learned that they were in Milici in Vlasenica, and to help there at this military farm in Branjevo about certain issues, but they didn't tell me exactly what it was about." And he goes further in his testimony to talk about his role in the executions with members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. So, Colonel, you've said that you have no knowledge of the killings, you don't know of the details of what the 10th Sabotage Unit was doing, on this day, the 16th of July in particular, and this witness directly contradicts you and puts you at the heart of staffing and directing the operation. You were there -- you were there with your operative unit in Banja Luka personally picking the people to go to Branjevo farm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon, Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, from the first to the last sentence everything that is stated here is a lie. I state that with full responsibility and I think that the court in Sarajevo did establish that it was a lie. The man who -- I don't know the man, I never saw him. He doesn't know me. I never saw him in my life. And that has nothing to do with it. These are just fabrications by Dusko Tomic's lawyer with that person and there are several, not just one. That absolutely, absolutely is not correct, none of it is. The 15th and the 16th, I think these are the dates, were the days when I was in Han Pijesak. I never went to Branjevo in my life, never ever. I know where it is on the map. Never ever. He also was saying about some vehicle, that we were going somewhere. In the end the lie was found out and ultimately I think that person needs to be tried because of those lies, but in any case he's already in Bijeljina, in prison, precisely because of fraud and lies and cheating. He also served prison time in Serbia and now he's serving prison time in Bijeljina and his lawyer is Dusko Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When then exactly did you come to learn about the killings at Srebrenica, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The participation of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The participation of the detachment in the killings?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what we're talking about? Or generally when?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When did you, head of intelligence for the VRS, under Colonel Tolimir, when did you come to learn about the killings in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something that appeared in the media, but I couldn't really tell you the exact date when that was. For the most part, my first information could only be after the actions were ended in the western sector prior to the Dayton Agreement. When I asked for an exchange to be carried out, exchange of our prisoners who happened to be in Muslim prisons in Zenica, and we would on our part release the prisoners that we had in Srebrenica. And I asked that we exchange ten of theirs for one of -- ten of ours for one of theirs, and I think General Tolimir said that we didn't have enough prisoners for such an action to be carried out in that way. As for the information received from the information media, it was clear that an execution had taken place. But until December, I did not know that this was something that soldiers from the 10th Detachment took part in. But as for finding out about it for the first time, I'm really unable to tell you the exact date when that was. And no one, let me just say that as well, no one, no one -- I did not hear it at the Main Staff from anyone. No one talked about that and nobody talked about it in units either where I would go. A lot of it came from the media from the outside, from the Muslim side. And later when the Belgrade media began to write about it. But I wouldn't be able to say exactly when these first reports about it began to emerge.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: During your testimony in the Mladic case last week, you talked with my colleague --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Vanderpuye about the operation, the killing operation, and the scope of the killing operation. And you said at transcript page 13103, in regard to the scale of the logistics of the operation: "I can't say that everybody knew. I can't say that. Most did. For example, some of my desk officers may have been unaware." And then you went on further: "But realistically speaking, yes, probably many people knew because it was a sizeable operation. These people needed to be transported, logistics units engaged, transport organised, engineering corps activated, so many people were probably engaged in it." And then at transcript pages 13125 to 13126 you also mentioned prisoners being taken through the zone as one of the reasons why people knew or had to know about the crimes. You said: "If it was being done during the day, people could probably see that, the way they moved, and some people certainly did," but you really couldn't say everyone. Some did probably. And then further on 13126 you agreed that people who had secured and guarded the prisoners could see the people being put on trucks or buses and being taken away. And you indicated that there were exchange commissions with the Main Staff and corps commissions for the exchange of prisoners and they were probably also informed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you, the head of intelligence, was not -- were not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the moment when everything was passing there. MUP was involved in order to regulate the traffic. They took part in the implementation, but I'm not aware of that. But I heard of the involvement of MUP units. Therefore, many people knew, but I suppose that many people were appalled by this and they simply did not talk about it. I did not hear a single word uttered at the command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please repeat your last sentence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be the reason why people kept quiet, to put it simply. They were appalled by hearing that. Some of them may not have even believed that it really happened, that they thought that it was just a media propaganda, and no one ever discussed this issue, not a single word was said in the Main Staff or elsewhere and nobody broached this subject at all anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just let's keep talking about logistics for a minute. When you talked in your testimony in the Mladic case about the killings, you were describing a large-scale operation that involved the movement of prisoners across military zones, it involved assets that had to be secured from different corps departments and ministries. It involved personnel from different organs and administrations. And your evidence is that that wasn't discussed at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Believe me, nobody talked about this. I'm telling you and I explained what was the probable reason for that. Maybe one or two persons discussed that privately, but nobody talked about this in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you would agree this kind of operation, this kind of -- the scope of this -- the logistical scope of this kind of operation implies some degree of higher level co-ordination, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably it involved that and you can see that people were being brought from different sectors and different zones, and so on and so forth. Requisitions were made for vehicles, fuel, maybe somebody asked for an explanation and somebody provided an explanation and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I normally wouldn't break but I am keeping an eye on the time, and I've just been notified I have ten minutes left in the allotted time which was awarded before this witness completed his testimony in the Mladic case. I wonder if I might, with Your Honours' leave, of course, be able to finish this area and then go back to the witness's presence in the enclave which we haven't had a chance to deal with yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in total, how much longer would you need from now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I hope the ten minutes from my original allotment and then something under 40 minutes there following, probably -- hopefully half an hour or between half an hour and 40 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, in total you're asking for 30 minutes or 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd appreciate if at all possibility some flexibility, Your Honour, and I would do my best to finish within an additional half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
