utterances.text: Yes, we are planning to take a break at quarter to 1.00, so please try to conclude by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll do my utmost, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, you just said -- we were talking about the co-ordination of assets from different sectors and zones, and you talked about requisitions made for vehicles and fuel and somebody providing an explanation. What level of decision-making and co-ordination does a logistics operation like this imply?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly, but most probably at the level of the corps because that was a corps operation, and it was up to the corps command to request from the logistics of the Main Staff some kind of materiel in order to reinforce the logistical support I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- concerning the regulation of traffic and groups and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's talk about the exhumations and reburials of the Bosnian Muslim men and boys who were killed at Branjevo, at Kozluk, at Petkovici dam, at Orahovac, and Glogova that happened in September and October 1995. This was a massive logistics effort and it involved the delivery of large amounts of fuel, the assignment of vehicles, excavators, trucks, people from across different military sectors, from different organs, including the police and the civilian authorities. There is no way that was corps-level decision, was it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that some aspects were resolved by the Main Staff logistical department.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, you're a senior intelligence officer with, by the time the war was over, 20 years' experience, you remained in the Main Staff. You were involved in meetings, briefing, and conversations with General Mladic and the assistant commanders and also with your counterparts all the way up until after the end of the war. You would have heard the international outcry for access to Serb-held territory through the eastern enclaves because that was your job to do and you've said that again and again. Your focus was strategic intelligence, and all you can say in response to this question was that it was possible?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me put this to you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Just a brief intervention. The witness said "yes" halfway through the question. Therefore, I would kindly ask Madam Edgerton to establish whether the answer "yes" pertains to the entire question that she put. He answered before the translation was finished and he answered yes midway through the question, which indicates apparently that he understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what I could add. I don't understand. Look, I told you that I left the area on the 18th of July. I was at home and in the hospital. General Mladic called me and I cut my sick leave short for a few days and he called me to come to Ostrelj. Croatia had already launched an attack on the Krajina and at the time we were focused and concentrated on those problems. Nobody was discussing any longer about what was going on and what had been going on until the completion of the Dayton Agreement. In this period prior to the Dayton Agreement, we were focused on this situation. And before the conclusion of the Dayton agreement I and a group of officers were sitting and preparing information that was necessary to conclude the Dayton Agreement. I'm not denying that there were some other activities at the same time, but my organ was focused and involved in what I just explained to you that we were doing and we were doing it around-the-clock.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 18 it should read: I'm not denying that there may have been other activities. [In English] "May have been" [Interpretation] "May have been" instead of, as it says here, that there were some other activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, you -- let me put this to you: You remained involved in intel work throughout the war. You were, after General Tolimir, the most senior -- the most senior intelligence officer in the VRS --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew because you were helping in the -- you were -- you knew because you were working in the Main Staff and with foreign officials on ways of getting the air-strikes to stop, you knew about the prospect of international deployment on VRS terrain, and your job was to keep - knowing that - your job was to keep the story of the killings outside of the public eye. And that's exactly what you were doing throughout --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General -- Colonel, pardon me, I keep giving you a promotion. But that's exactly what you did, Colonel, you covered up the story of the killings when you issued -- when you made sure some of the participants in the Branjevo farm executions were issued with false IDs by your services together with the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Please, no. That was not the aim and that's not it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the objective was --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, just before you answer --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for those people --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before you answer, let's have a look at your order regarding the ID cards. It's P4491. You saw it during your testimony last week.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, this is document which is coded, marked very urgent, from you personally to Dragan Kijac, and it's dated 16 January 1996, says: "Considering that we have a group of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who are foreign citizens or are on the list of individuals ... indicted by the Hague Tribunal, we ask you to order the Bijeljina MUP to issue personal IDs with Serb names to them or with different names for Serb nationals ..." And if we go down in English, you can see it in B/C/S, but if we go to the bottom of the page in English, I'm sorry, it must be on the second page in English. The very -- the note at the bottom of this document says to Mr. Kijac: "You are required to act on this request by the VRS Main Staff." So I'd like to hear your explanations about why this isn't a cover-up, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it in the original document, the registering of the persons and so on and so forth. And please report back about your decision, no. We sat down once I received the information from Pelemis about the participation and we made an assessment about the general safety and security of those people. We also had information that some people from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't understand the word used by the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you in the middle of your answer, but the interpreters didn't understand one of the words that you used. I wouldn't normally interrupt you mid-answer like this, but to make sure they understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat your answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not the goal. The goal was to have these people stay there and to be brought before justice. Instead of someone else taking up this role on themselves and kill these people in order to clear up the situation. That is why this document was written and sent to the ministry. At the time when we sent it to the ministry, and we immediately indicated which specific people were in question because The Hague Prosecution was not yet initiating any investigation of those people at this level, but we wanted the minister to know the identity of those people. In addition, we provided a list of the people so that they can be located if a need arose and to be relocated from their then-places of residence to other streets and residence places and that was the objective. We wanted to avoid someone else taking that prerogative into their own hands and resolving this issue in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But that's not what this document says.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't go into detail in this. I discussed this with the minister. This document went through several different levels and it's not very simple exactly like this, it's not so easy to write it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you discussed these perpetrators personally with Dragan Kijac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan Kijac knew the identity of those people. He gave his approval, and he kept a list. So there is very precise records of the names of the people and people who did not participate there were also on the list -- actually, were not participating in that group, but there was -- there were people of interest and we undertook upon ourselves to relocate them to different addresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. AID was not recorded, AID is a Muslim secret service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The majority of the persons were from the area of the Federation and they were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your explanation as to the mention of indictments by the Hague Tribunal is to the effect that -- well, actually, it looks like, based on your explanation, the contents of this document with reference to the indictments by the Hague Tribunal is nothing more than misinformation. So the -- there's false information in this document that you used to get false IDs for these people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, madam. No. This is put here -- let me tell you now. At that moment, I thought it was horrible to say that these people committed such and such crimes. So in order for one to understand what this is all about, I said that those were persons, and I quote literally, persons against whom indictments were issued by the Hague Tribunal but no indictments were issued at the time against any of them, not at that particular time. Perhaps with regard to Erdemovic there was some information, I don't know, but I formulated it in this way in order to help the minister understand who this referred to, who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: People who he needed to hide; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, not to hide. He had a list of people, but not people to hide but to provide them with safe shelter in order to avoid being executed. AID was looking for three or four of them and we wanted to prevent that from being done. We just wanted this to go through regular proceedings. We just didn't want anyone taking law into their own hands and doing harm to those people. That was the sole reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So instead --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel said that those who took them to do the assignment should not be executed, that means by those who had given them assignment, that was not recorded. And then the next sentence pertains to the danger that was coming from the AID. [In English] It could be clarified what Colonel meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it reads well as it is now. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this document doesn't say a word about AID; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no mention there. I didn't mention anyone else. Please, this document was encoded, I submitted to the Bijeljina municipal SUP, and then it went through different levels. That's why I didn't put it, but I wanted the minister to know what this was all about and I expected him to give his approval, but I wanted him to know exactly which persons we were referring to and their exact location. So if any court of law was looking for them, they would know where they were. That was on the 16th of January when the border was porous, when there were no troops guarding the border any longer. And that was an additional risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, Colonel, I'd like to go back to the 13th of July and your trip into the enclaves ostensibly to deliver some information to either General Tolimir or General Mladic. I'd like to know, first of all, because you've never actually said it, who did you meet in Belgrade to get the information that was so urgent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to give you a name? Please, I can't do that. It's a person with whom I maintained contacts and who provided us with the necessary intelligence. That's one thing. Secondly, I told you I had a meeting with the Japanese military envoy, maybe with an Italian one as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, your statement doesn't say anything about any of the people that you met with in Belgrade, so that's why I'd like to know. Did they -- and the Japanese military envoy and the Italian one both spoke to you about the situation with respect to the prisoners of war in Srebrenica, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The discussion was how the operation was already over and the focus was shifted to Croatia, what would happen there, and about the imminent attack, and they knew about that. They knew what our views were about that and which measures we intended to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now something --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: August/September -- excuse me. Secondly, the peace process was over on the date when we wrote this, but as for the 13th of July they were interested to hear what our plans were in the event of Croatia occupying the Republic of Serbian Krajina proceed to attack Republika Srpska. And the person that I mentioned is, let's say -- let's call him an agent, and he was registered under a special code-name which I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, the thing that's -- Colonel --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it doesn't really matter either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The thing that's always puzzled me, Colonel, is that when you received this information that was so urgent, why you didn't make your way to the western front where General Milovanovic was already operational to give him that information instead of going down to the eastern enclaves? The person who needed that information more than any one of your commanders was General Milovanovic. So why didn't you go there instead of going down to the enclaves if the information was so urgent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the commander who ultimately makes the decision. General Milovanovic does things that are current matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure your last sentence was translated because you spoke with your microphone off, but let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision, the final decision, is made by the commander. General Milovanovic is the Chief of Staff. He was in charge of those units there, but also there was a series of other actions and manoeuvres that the commander has to decide about, and that is why I went there and because I thought that we had little time and that what was ahead of us were major problems, enormous problems, and our -- my personal opinion was that we should go as soon as possible, leave Srebrenica, the corps is finishing that, that operation is done and over with militarily, and let us seek a solution in the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So rather than go there urgently, you went there via Bijeljina, via Nova Kasaba, via Bratunac, where you stopped at the brigade command, via Potocari, and then found General Mladic in Srebrenica; right? You stopped four places along the way before you actually went to your commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for my commander. I came and from Bijeljina I went straight to look for my commander, and I asked there where he was. I didn't know where he was. I know that he's in the area of Srebrenica, somewhere in that area. That is a theatre that involves a broader area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I went to the military police battalion, so that the commander could tell me where General Mladic is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. He is barely audible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, when you answer my questions, I think you will help the interpreters if you can try and lean forward a little bit into the microphones. Colonel, as an intelligence officer, you recognised that the situation at Nova Kasaba and Sandici, where you saw hundreds of prisoners, had massive intel potential, and you were in a unique situation where you came face-to-face with the prisoners who had survived and up until that point surrendered. Isn't it the case, Colonel, that you went there -- the real reason why you went there was to see and hear for yourself what information had been gathered, how many people who had surrendered, who had surrendered, to find out how big the column of 15.000 men and boys leaving -- of military age leaving Srebrenica actually was, who had been armed, what communications they had with the 2nd Corps, you went to Nova Kasaba and passed through Sandici because you were doing your job? You were gathering intel on the prisoners. You, as the senior intel guy in the Bosnian Serb army Main Staff, were checking in to make sure the process was going on as it should?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I never received any kind of assignments like that from anyone, the ones that you mentioned to me just now. I was not interested in that at all. I do not have any information there that would be important to me that I could get from some soldier who would be arrested. And now if I were to ask is there an officer there, if I were to ask whether they were identified or not, Srebrenica is done and over with militarily as far as I'm concerned. The rest is just a routine matter. It was supposed to be taken care of in a routine manner, the prisoners of war were supposed to be taken to a camp for POWs, and then they're supposed to be processed and interviewed, and this is of greater interest for the security service, not for my service. From these soldiers, my service could not get anything, not even from their officers, whereas they can -- these other people can look for perpetrators of war crimes, and so on and so forth, in different operations that the forces from Srebrenica carried out in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your statement, Colonel, at paragraph 12 and page 15 in English and page 10 in your language, you said: "When I reached Srebrenica, I found General Mladic and explained the situation to him." But when you testified in the Mladic case last week at transcript page 13054, you said that you met General Mladic at Potocari. Are you trying to hide the fact that you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in Srebrenica at all. I was never in that area, and really when I came there I thought that I was on the periphery of Srebrenica. And only when I talked to -- actually, when I saw the picture, what was behind the buildings, I showed that to the investigator of The Hague Tribunal in Banja Luka, and then I said, "No, that's where I was, that's it. What is this?" And then he said to me, "No, this is Potocari." So I was in Potocari, I was not in Srebrenica. I was not in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at your statement, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And unfortunately I don't have the exhibit number off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3720, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Could we have a look, please, at D3720, at page 15 in English and page 10 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, look at the third full paragraph of the page on the screen in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why is it so blurry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please carry on. I was watching the monitor, video. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Look at the third full paragraph, Colonel, on the page in front of you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It says: "When I reached Srebrenica, I found General Mladic and explained the situation to him ..." Are you saying -- are you saying that the statement you signed is wrong?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I made a mistake. I confused things. I thought it was Srebrenica but it wasn't Srebrenica. And when I saw the picture -- I mean, the person who took the picture and the building that is behind the back. I was never in Srebrenica. I mean, I thought that it was there. I never was in Srebrenica. I mean from some distance. And then later I gave this statement during the next conversation with the investigator. Now I cannot remember his name, I'll remember that too, and then I asked that that be corrected in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, if you had been to Srebrenica, you would have seen the body of the man in the town centre whose throat had been slit by a man from your 10th Sabotage Detachment on the order of Milorad Pelemis. Is that why you're now insisting that you weren't in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I hear from you now, that that was ordered to him, that this person's throat was slit. No, that's not the reason. I was not in Srebrenica. Do you understand that? These prisoners were all gathered in Potocari at the base there. That's where the buses came, trucks towards the end, and that's where women, children, and so on were loaded onto buses and that's where I was and I didn't go any further than that. And that's recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm keeping an eye on the time. I recognise my undertaking and my best efforts. I do feel I would like to go a little bit further with this witness and show him a video that he's seen previously and not had an opportunity to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What video?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A video of the witness in Srebrenica with General Mladic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think the clip takes about two minutes all together, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break after that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have -- I'd like to play a clip now from the Srebrenica trial video which is P4201, part 3, from the video V0009016, time codes 0008 to 0241. And I hope my colleagues in the booth have received their transcripts for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "You see, unfortunately, your camera too can testify to this. This was destroyed probably sometime in 1992 or 1993, just like everything else that was Serb in Srebrenica and around it, as far as Muslim forces and followers of Alija Izetbegovic were able to reach. I have seen for myself today that our authority has been established here in Srebrenica, and you saw over there that an evacuation was carried out of all those who wanted to leave Srebrenica safely. The entire former enclave of Srebrenica is under the control of the forces of the Republika Srpska army. We are at the old Orthodox church in Srebrenica. It was destroyed and turned into a stable. Well, I am archpriest Nedeljko Mitrovic, priest from Bratunac, and this church is dedicated to the shroud of the Holy Madonna. Today, the 13th of July, 1995, this church has finally been liberated. "Are you from here? "Yes, I am. From this house. "From this house? "Yes. "When were you expelled in from here? "On 10th April 1992. "Is there anything inside? Have you been inside? "Yes, I have. "Let's go in for a while. This is your own house? "It's my own house. "They have destroyed all of this? "All of it. I just got in through the gate. "Did" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a -- shall we stop here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We heard something that is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While they were translating, they couldn't hear you, Mr. Salapura. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there when this conversation with this woman took place. That recording does exist and then there's also the part with the journalist. That is after the talk with the journalist and then Mladic talked to this woman. And together with this investigator from The Hague Tribunal, I mean he told me that that was Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I was asking just what you said. Please carry on, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's only a few more seconds of film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But then we might have to hear what our friends the interpreters have heard that's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need to play a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And do you know where he was buried. "I don't know that either. "What kind of work did you do in Srebrenica before the war? What is your educational background? "Secondary school of economics. "Secondary school of economics."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance. The missing part is precisely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "He was killed. "Yes. "And do you know where he was buried? "I don't know that either. "What kind of work did you do in Srebrenica before the war here at the revenue administration?"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, the time code that we've just stopped at is 2:34.6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, that's you in behind the woman on the screen right now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, General Mladic is in Srebrenica, he says he's in Srebrenica, he's in landmarks of Srebrenica, he asks the woman who is on the screen with him if she's from there and she agrees, and your evidence is that this is all happening in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said in my first variant that I found General Mladic in Srebrenica, and then the investigator, your investigator, showed me the recording of this conversation with General Mladic, where behind you can see a building. And then he said, "Is that it?" And I said, "Yes." And then he said, "Well, that's not Srebrenica, that is Potocari." That's the first time I came there. Do you understand that? And when we set out from there, then General Milovanovic, together with this woman, went there and he -- she took him to her house. We all went there. There were several of us and these cameramen and his security detail and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I believe Mladic -- the witness said Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness said Milovanovic, Dr. Karadzic. The witness should be asked to correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mladic. Yes, Mladic, General Mladic. Milovanovic was not there. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one more very short clip, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, and this is from P4201, part 2, time code 17:59 to 19:05.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll leave it, Your Honours. It was the wrong clip and I think it's best to leave it given the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.40. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good day, Excellencies. Good day to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I shall start with the latest. On page 55 of today's transcript, it was suggested to you that there had to be talks about POWs from Srebrenica between yourself and the military attaches of Japan and Italy. When was it that you saw these attaches, on which day, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 12th of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until then, on the basis of what you know now, until then had something happened that would have had to be the subject of your conversations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know then. I left from Banja Luka, as I said I was on sick leave. I did not know at all what was happening in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica. I only found out in Modrica when I arrived. They told me that our units had taken Srebrenica, liberated Srebrenica, and so on. So that is where I received this first information -- well -- so I had nothing to say to them about Srebrenica or in relation to Srebrenica, I mean in that contact. The talks had to do with a completely different subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of what you found out subsequently and what you know now, do you think that they could have had any knowledge of the killings on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot speculate and I don't think so. They didn't ask me anything about that. On the 11th the operation in Srebrenica was over. So on the 12th, I don't know, were there killings on the 12th? I did not see anywhere en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a brief question. What do reconnaissance/sabotage detachments do in any army otherwise?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They go into reconnaissance missions; that is to say, they reconnoitre the enemy forces starting with the front end and going in depth. And now it depends on the units themselves what the depth may be. At any rate, in our situation it was 5 or 6 kilometres in depth into the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, also carrying out sabotage activities. We in the Army of Republika Srpska had just this one sabotage unit that was capable of carrying out such operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us approximately from the beginning until the end of the war how many prisoners of war we had and before July 1995 how many times executions or killings of prisoners of war took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't see how this arises from the cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the cross-examination called into question whether people knew of the executions and whether it had happened in the past would also be relevant to whether someone would know or expect that these prisoners would be executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, actually, I don't -- I didn't follow the question. What was your question, Mr. Karadzic, from the beginning until the end of war?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until July 1995, how many POWs did we have and how many times did executions, unlawful killings, take place before July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of a single case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although the Trial Chamber knows already, could you tell us, though, where it was to be expected that these prisoners of war would have gone? Where were they supposed to be put up?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was deeply convinced that they would be in POW camps. As far as I can remember, that is to say up until now in that area, in 1992, Susica, there was some camp there near Vlasenica and there was a rather large camp in Bijeljina, in Batkovic, that was properly set up for normal life. Then there was Manjaca near Banja Luka, and I don't know whether in the Herzegovina Corps there was one and around Sarajevo, down there, what was the name of that? Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kula?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in 1995 in the area of Eastern Bosnia, the eastern part of Republika Srpska, there was another camp that had been properly set up?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Batkovic, yes, and it had the largest capacity too. I personally had never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us if prisoners were to be transported to Batkovic, where would they pass along the route from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would need to go through Zvornik to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then from Bijeljina to Batkovic through the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were talking and you were asked about the transport people, so trucks and buses. This action of transporting people from the north from -- towards Batkovic, was it something unusual or something that would alarm those who saw it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transport itself probably would not. All that would be seen would be that there was a large number of prisoners, a mass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were asked on the first day about contacts and if it says there "call Salapura" and there is a tick saying that Salapura was called, does that mean that they actually reached you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because I don't remember much today. I don't remember many of those contacts today. By phone mostly it was conveying messages that were left perhaps from the level of the president's office or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from the Presidency, was I the only person that you communicated with? Did you have contacts with Subotic, Koljevic, Plavsic, or anyone else from the president's office?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in contact with all members of the Presidency, perhaps more with Koljevic than with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know who all of my secretaries worked for, who did they make calls for, who did they receive calls for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever inform me verbally or in writing that prisoners from Srebrenica were executed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I said that and I stand by that today, that I did not know that until late and that was not part of my duties, it was not part of my remit. There are other services that would deal with that, with instances like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Colonel, sir, did you know anyone, either myself or anyone to the lowest-ranking state instance, if anyone had an intention or plan to commit genocide or to expel Muslims and Croats from the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of such a plan. No one ever told me about such a plan, I never heard of such a plan, and as far as I am concerned a plan like that would merely be the result of a sick mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there other -- in our army were there people who were not of Serb ethnicity? Were there other non-Serbs, Muslims, Croats, Slovenians, what was the ethnic composition of our army? Who were all the ethnic -- what were all the ethnic groups in our ranks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were others. I couldn't tell you exactly who, but all the minorities that lived in our territory were a part of the army, the Serb ethnic group was absolutely dominant, though, but there were others to a small degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your opinion and according to what you know, would the unlawful killing of prisoners at the end of the war be in the interest of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not in the interest of Republika Srpska. At the end of the war, then, and now I think it created more damage to the Serbian people than harm to the people from whose ranks those prisoners came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir, for your efforts and for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're ready to hear the evidence of Cedomir Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not Zametica?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zametica was postponed until the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Zelenovic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Zelenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have more or less understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you, and myself included, please speak slowly, speak our sentences out slowly and make a pause between question and answer so that everything could be recorded in the transcript. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D9682 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the screen in front of you, the Serbian version is on the left-hand side. Can you see the statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you read and sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did both read it and sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers essentially be the same as the ones in this statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the statement, Your Honours, pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it, but subject to portions of paragraph 24 which the Chamber has difficulty in following its meaning. It reads -- parts of it reads: "The president of the Crisis Staff, Brano Grujic, gave him a negative answer, and, in addition, told him that could not secure provisions for the men who would keep people the freed parts of the town." So I would like you, Mr. Karadzic, to lead live that part if you wish us to tender that part as well. Yes, shall we assign the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3723, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am now going to read the summary of Mr. Cedo Zelenovic's statement in English. [In English] Cedo Zelenovic worked as an engineer in the management of the aluminosilicate plant in Zvornik since 1975. Relations between the Muslims and Serbs in Zvornik were good before the first multi-party elections. In 1991, the SDA Zvornik came under pressure from the SDA leadership in Sarajevo to implement SDA policy on the secession of BH from Yugoslavia. In October 1991, the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo out-voted the Serbs and proclaimed the sovereignty of BH. This was a clear signal that the Serbs were socially, culturally, and ethnically at risk. The Serbs in BH established regional areas and municipalities, and this was the only way to protect themselves and challenge the chauvinistic and separatist activities of the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia. The poor state of inter-ethnic relations was reflected in the factory where Cedo Zelenovic worked. In 1991 it was apparent that Muslims and Serbs were forming their own groups in offices. When talking to their Muslim colleagues, Serbs were repeatedly told that they had Serbia, and had no business looking for anything in BH. Muslims strongly opposed the Cutileiro Plan after accepted. Alija Izetbegovic rejected the Cutileiro Plan because he enjoyed the support of the United States. There were countless stupidities in interpretations and relations among employees. Serbs taught by their experience from Second World War sought protection from the regular forces of JNA. The Muslim leadership on its path of chauvinists and separatism saw the JNA as an obstacle, so they portrayed it to its people in a planned and systematic fashion as an occupational and Chetnik force. Two soldiers were physically attacked in a Muslim village close to Kalesija because they were members of the JNA. In December 1991, the Crisis Staff was formed. It was not operational except until 6th to 10th of April, 1992, when the interim government of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik was formed. In March 1992, owing to the escalation of inter-ethnic conflicts, Muslim fundamentalists in Zvornik mistreated a number of Serbian residents. Elderly Serbs were attacked and physically mistreated. A JNA officer was attacked. Muslim flags were put on buildings and groups of Muslim youths imbibed with nationalism moved about the town carrying religious flags and cassette players with loud music. After the Muslim-Croatian referendum for the independence of BH, anti-Serbian hysteria started in BH and Zvornik. Muslim and Croatian flags were tied together at all political and sporting events. All was directed against the national interests of the Serbs in the municipality. The Serbian leadership, headed by Radovan Karadzic, did its best to calm the situation and avoid the conflict. Karadzic asked that the leadership in Zvornik to negotiate with the Muslims and find peaceful solutions to problems. A rally was organised in the town hall. Karadzic and Muslim leader Zulfikarpasic said that BH should remain in Yugoslavia and arrangements needed to be made to avoid a war at all costs. In the internal organisation of BH should have been in line with agreements between ethnic groups and for the benefit of all who lived in it. Karadzic was committed to a peaceful solution to the problems in Bosnia. People from the SDA were unhappy that Zulfikarpasic advocated a peaceful solution and had therefore set up an ambush on the way between Zvornik and Sarajevo where they were going to assassinate him. The Zvornik SDS and SDA leaders negotiated a peaceful division of Zvornik. While negotiating -- negotiations were ongoing, the chief of the SUP of police approved and armed the reserve police which were staffed exclusively with Muslims. On 5th of April, 1992, in Sapna, armed Muslim extremists carried out a terrorist attack on a JNA vehicle in passing. A JNA officer and a soldier were killed and the rest of those found in the vehicle were taken captive. The attack in Sapna was the reason to seal off Zvornik and all the villages where they were the majority population, as well as some bridges from the town to Serbia. The Crisis Staff in Karakaj was convened after a number of Serbs fled to Serbia from Zvornik. A group of Muslim soldiers guarded the bridge in Zvornik. Under the pretext of looking for weapons, armed Muslims searched Serbian homes. Serbs were bullied and physically mistreated. Arkan's soldiers beat up two Serbian negotiators in Mali Zvornik. The Zvornik Serbian leadership had been trying to resolve the situation peacefully. Arkan prevented the negotiations from proceeding, so he took over all the power and personally commanded his forces in the operation to lift the blockade. The Crisis Staff did not make a decision on lifting the blockade from Zvornik; Arkan did this. After the blockade was lifted, local authorities were established, but they did not have any power because of the number of paramilitaries and individuals. Paramilitaries introduced the reign of terror. All residents of Zvornik were mistreated. Paramilitaries seized the town and made all decisions on the basis of their fighting strength and power. Muslim extremists planted explosives under the factory's red sludge piping above a drain, polluting the Sapna river and killing a huge number of fish. They also planted 70 kilos of explosives in the spillway tunnel. If activated, an unprecedented environmental disaster would occur. On 27th of May, 1992, Muslim extremists attacked a column of trucks carrying ore to Cedo Zelenovic's factory killing five innocent and unarmed drivers. More trucks and more people were massacred after this event and after which production was suspended. Only after Zuco, Repic, and their paramilitaries were arrested in late July 1992 were relatively normal conditions created for the local authorities. All the arrested paramilitaries were brought to justice and supposedly convicted of their own crimes and offences mainly in Serbia. [Interpretation] That would be the summary of Mr. Zelenovic's statement. I have no questions for him at this time except for those that you indicated. So I would kindly ask that the witness be permitted to use his own statement if he has it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, do you have your statement in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When leading live, I would like you to put the question directly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what was the request by Arkan to Grujic and the Serbian authorities in Zvornik and what the reaction of the authorities was?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Arkan's request, Arkan and his assistant Peja's request was for us to decide at the Crisis Staff to lift the blockade of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the answer of the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Our response, the response of the Crisis Staff at the time one or two days before the conflict broke out, was that we were still trying to resolve things in a peaceful way and that we could not make that decision like that, nor were there any forces that would be able to help them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, the interpreters were not able to hear the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the answer has now been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you not say that there were no forces that would be able to help them, the ones that they were requesting? That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Other than the decision to lift the blockade, what else did they request from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they asked for police forces which -- well, at that time the police had separated. The Serbian police was in Karakaj, not all of them, just those who stayed there, and these others probably left. Thus, to help them in this lifting of the blockade of Zvornik. And they received the answer that I mentioned a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this now sufficient, satisfactory, Your Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's for you to present your evidence. Very well. Mr. Zelenovic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its most part in writing, that is, your witness statement. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. McKenna. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an intervention here. I saw in English where these explosions were, where this explosion was planted. It says "red sludge," but actually it's red mud, "crveni mulj." I just wanted to make that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenovic. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 19 of your statement, you discussed the negotiations which took place between the SDS and the SDA in Zvornik. I'd just like to clarify. Is this a reference to the negotiations that were taking place in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could you please put this variant -- could you please put the Serbian version of my statement on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In hard copy I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I have nothing. I was told that I would be given everything here and that I should not bring anything with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, your statement will be forthcoming to you, but in the meantime read it from the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So it's just the first sentence of paragraph 19 of your statement, Mr. Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And can you just clarify that this is a reference to the negotiations which were taking place in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: That should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And so you state, also in paragraph 19, that while the negotiations were ongoing, Muslim reserve police in Zvornik were armed. And at paragraph 14 of your statement you say that the Crisis Staff was not operational until the 6th of April, 1992. It's true, though, isn't it, Mr. Zelenovic, that Serb municipality leaders were organising for war before the Crisis Staff was formally operational on the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Look, I was a member of the Crisis Staff that was set up sometime in December and it says here it has certain functions for a few days, with a view to calming down the situation and that was prior the arrival of those paramilitaries. And it basically became non-operational. As for the preparations for war, I'm not aware of that. What I do know are these things and that is that in the then-Bosnia and Herzegovina when Bosnia seceded from the former Yugoslavia and after the negotiations about the internal set-up of Bosnia failed, the only thing that Serbs could do was to form autonomous districts comprising two or three municipalities or only one municipality. Now, if you would describe that as preparations for war, I would rather say that that was preparation for peace. Throughout the First and the Second World War, the Serbs suffered a lot and were victims of heinous crimes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: -- and in the Second World War --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry, I'm going to have to interrupt you here. We are very limited in time, so I'm going to ask you to focus very carefully on the questions that I'm asking you and answer them as concisely and precisely as possible. Now, I understand your evidence to be that you weren't aware that the Crisis Staff was involved in organising for war in early 1992. And I'd like to show you a document on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P3390.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] In line 14, page 82, the witness said that the Crisis Staff was suspended by the paramilitary, that it was the paramilitary who suspended the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Zelenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please see page 19 of the English of this document and page 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, you'll see, Mr. Zelenovic, that this is a report on the work of the Zvornik SJB for the year 1992. I'd like to turn to page 21 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S now. And halfway down this page it says -- there's a passage that reads: "As agreed upon with the Crisis Staff, a meeting was organised with active and reserve policemen of Serb nationality in Celopek in late March 1992. A certain number of young people from Celopek and Trisic were also invited to the meeting. Over 150 Serbs attended the meeting, assignments were handed out regarding the putting up of barricades at certain locations, as well as on all other roads running across Serb territories, securing of all important facilities in the Karakaj industrial zone, and seizing of the bridges in Karakaj and Sepak. Active SJB personnel were given concrete assignments concerning the extraction of vehicles and other materiel and technical equipment ..." Now, were you aware that this meeting had taken place?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, if we could move to the previous page, which is page 20 in the English and page 17 in the B/C/S. And we see under the heading (a) which reads: "Description of Activities Undertaken on the Winning Over of Personnel for the Serb MUP by 4th of April, 1992." It says three paragraphs down: "Working on various check-points during the months of January and February, police personnel of Serb nationality enabled the transport of weapons, ammunition, and other materiel and technical equipment necessary for the arming of the Serb people in this territory of this municipality." Now, were you aware that police personnel of Serb nationalities were enabling the arming of Serb people in Zvornik in January and February 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that at all. This is the first that I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zelenovic, your colleague Mr. Jovan Ivanovic recently confirmed to the Trial Chamber that before the war meetings took place, including in Celopek, in which the Serb leadership in Zvornik organised the arming of the Serbs in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And for the parties' reference that's T 39852 to 39855.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So it's a fact, isn't it, that the Crisis Staff, even if it was not formally operational until the 6th of April, Serb municipality leaders were organising for war well before that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be one and the same question apparently. As far as my activities on the Crisis Staff are concerned in which I acted as a member of a charity society, this was not mentioned in any of these meetings. This was only activated, as it says here, I don't know the 4th, the 5th, or the 6th, as it is stated in the statement, and I wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: I mean -- I'm sorry. Everything could be either true or untrue. I cannot vouch for that because I myself was not active in that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now at paragraph 26 of your statement you describe how Arkan took over all the power and personally commanded his forces in the operation to lift the blockade of Zvornik, and you state that in these battles he was joined by individuals and groups who came from Serbia and Croatia. And in paragraph 35 of your statement you say that you never heard that the paramilitaries were invited in by anyone from the Crisis Staff. Now, we'll come back to the issue of who invited the paramilitaries in, but it's a fact, isn't it, that the Zvornik authorities were supportive of Arkan and groups from Serbia coming into Zvornik, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, let me tell you this. The Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. We didn't understand what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Ivanovic. Could you start your answer again? The interpreters did not understand what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime, I don't know, the whole time since the sovereign Bosnia was created, the Serbs were leaving and moving out of Zvornik, which left only 5 per cent of Serbs on the eve of the war, which is some 5.000 according to the 1991 census, but people didn't run away as a whim. They had to take their families away, they had to enrol their children in different schools, they felt threatened --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, I'm sorry, again that's not responsive to my question. I've asked you whether -- whether the Zvornik authorities were supportive of Arkan and groups from Serbia coming into Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Look, whether it was the authorities or not, I was on the Crisis Staff. I can tell you that I would have supported Satan himself if it would have helped to calm down the situation. You must realise if there was some force from above that could force everyone to look and find a peaceful solution, then you can call it support and that applies to the authorities as well instead of going out and killing each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So do you agree that the government was supportive -- that the Serb authorities were supportive of the paramilitaries coming in, just to clarify your evidence on this point?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Look, whether there was supporting or not, there are two things. One thing is to support conflict as a means of solving a problem and it's a completely different thing to support a so-called armed force coming in, in order to establish some kind of balance because the Serbs were vulnerable and threatened and by applying this force to compel and make the other side to agree to the peace. It was not like you describe it. Your question, whether they were supportive, they were supportive in the sense that I tried to explain to you and that is to avoid a conflict. Your question was something else and I said that we would have supported any force, be it paramilitary or some other, just to have the problem solved in order to avoid conflict. We didn't want the problem to be solved to the benefit of the Serbs, but we wanted to resolve this kind of ignorant attitude of the Muslim authorities which was prevalent practically from the date Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised and when the leadership headed by Alija Izetbegovic ignored all possible proposals, including the Cutileiro Plan. And what happened, I saw something as coming from heaven above, and I don't understand why this is being to vehemently opposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We're going to come to discuss some of the specific types of support that were provided, but let's just look at some of the individuals who were involved. So you've laid a lot of emphasis on Arkan's role. Could we please see 65 ter number 25239.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 20 to 22, it is unclear. The witness said that he had seen Cutileiro's Plan as something coming from the heaven above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's there. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zelenovic, if you look at the photograph of Mr. Karadzic on the screen, can you read what it says behind him?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Patron Saint's Day of MUP, St. Archangel Michael, Zvornik, can you move it a bit, I suppose it's 1995. You can't see the next digit. I suppose it's 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So it's clear that this celebration of the MUP patron saint took place after the Serb take-over of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Can you tell me the year next to the word "Zvornik"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We're unfortunately unable to move the photograph, but it's clear that it's 90 something. Do you agree that this would be after the take-over of Zvornik, given the context of the celebration?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I -- what I see is 95, it's nothing then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So could we now see 65 ter number 25240.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say "then it has nothing to do with this." [In English] "What I see is 1995, it's nothing then," "is nothing then" connected with -- [Interpretation] He said that it has nothing to do with the take-over of Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters are interpreting only what they hear witness saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, do you recognise the person at the podium in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And so it's clear these photos show, don't they, that Arkan continued to be received and supported by the local and indeed the republican leadership well after the take-over of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Look, let us go back to the question that you asked me a while ago, again in relation to Arkan. I personally, and I believe some of the local authorities, the SDS and so on, not "so on," the authorities themselves genuinely saw in Arkan a force that would establish a balance from the Serbian side in order to resolve things in a peaceful way. On the eve of the conflict itself, there were negotiations in that respect and it is common knowledge that he even, I don't know, beat up those Serbian representatives who were in negotiations with the representatives of the Muslim side. In that sense, you understand; but otherwise, nothing could be solved unless there was a balance imposed from the Serbian side and an increase of power which the Serbian authorities were unable to achieve and control. So things started going their own way. All of this came as an outcome of the rejection by the Muslims to negotiate. That is what caused the conflict and the ball started rolling. You have --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: -- to understand these are the Balkans we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenovic. I think again we are slightly straying from the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender those two photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although ... although -- I do apologise, Your Honours. I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll receive this, both these photos.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6412 and P6413 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can move on. Yes, Ms. McKenna, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, we've been discussing --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I do apologise. I wanted to intervene in relation to this photograph. Once again, if possible ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will ask you further questions. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We've been discussing Arkan's role in the take-over, but additional to Arkan and his men the operation to take over Zvornik was also carried out by the Serb TO and by Serb SJB personnel, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: During the deblockade, could you just clarify the question? During this conflict, the deblockade of Zvornik. Could you clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My question is: In addition to Arkan and his men, forces from the Serb TO and the Serb SJB were also involved in this operation, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Who took part? I really cannot give you an answer to that. I don't know. I mean as far as Serb forces are concerned of the police, that's probably that SJB -- no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P3390 again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is the police report that we've looked at earlier, and this time I'm interested in page 22 of the English and page 19 of the B/C/S. And you'll see, Mr. Zelenovic, that two paragraphs down in the B/C/S it states: "SJB personnel acting together with forces of the Serb TO entered Zvornik and took hold of the town's vital facilities on 8th of April, 1992." So do you agree that according to this contemporaneous document, forces of the Serb SJB and the Serb TO were involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. I mean, they came after the operation, and of course there has to be a take-over and some kind of order has to be established and these same forces and the authorities later on called upon everyone to return to Zvornik. You have to know that too, and the way you put it, it doesn't have to mean that they took part. These forces, I mean, were so weak -- I mean, it's the Serb police, right? It's only natural that they should come to establish some kind of order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't mean what you said, that they took part in the conflict. I wasn't doing any counting and I didn't look at who was participating. I just know who made the decision. I've already said that and who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's talk about who -- the type of order that was established after, you say, the blockade was lifted. Now, at paragraph 28 of your statement you discuss that after the blockade was lifted, the local authorities were established but that to your knowledge those authorities didn't have any power. Now, I'd just like to clarify with you, you also say that after four days in the Crisis Staff you didn't join the government, but rather you went back to your work in the factory. So you're not really in a position to speak to the power that the authorities had over the paramilitaries, are you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, the way you put this is as if I did not want to take part in government. I had major responsibility in the factory in that situation, I mean, for work to go on. Practically I was there on the 6th I think, and I no longer showed up in these -- well, I mean the Crisis Staff stopped operating and I had my duties at the factory. And I what happened, I mean, after that -- I mean, well, I cannot go into detail since I'm not a member of government and since I wasn't anything special out there, didn't take part --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: -- as a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But you do, however, in your statement talk about the fact that the paramilitaries, and this is -- I'm referring to paragraph 30 in your statement, the paramilitaries in effect seized power in the town and made all the decisions on the basis of their strength and power and so this is why the local authorities could not stand up to them. And I'd just like to explore with you the relationship between the local authorities and the paramilitaries. You mention a number of times in your statement the Yellow Wasps and Zuco and Repic. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that the Yellow Wasps was the informal name of the Igor Markovic unit. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea whatsoever. I tried to stay away from these paramilitaries and Zuco. I had personal experience with him in the factory and that is not -- that is not in this condensed version. So he came to the factory and he wanted to make an armoured train out after an engine. One was in working order and the other one was not. And I said, "Okay, give him the one that didn't work," and I almost paid with my own life, and I stayed away from them. I know because I talked to people who were in power that it was impossible, that you couldn't resolve anything with them.
